body: Like I mentioned on the proposal, I'm not entirely sure this is the right way to go. We could also re-implement the aligned versions in godot-cpp using the existing `mem_alloc` function (and friends) that we already have

In the proposal's motivation, you wrote:

> A fluid simulation written in GDExtension that tries to make use of compiler vectorization for performance.

Does vectorization necessitate these functions?

Also, keep in mind that GDExtension is not only used by godot-cpp, but also many other languages: Swift, Go, Kotlin, Rust... and in the future even C#. Can those languages benefit from the APIs too? Or if we need fast allocations, would those rather use language-specific allocators or allocator schemes (e.g. arenas/pools)? The latter could bypass FFI overhead and adapt to the language itself (Swift e.g. uses ref-counting, while Kotlin/C# have a GC).

> Can those languages benefit from the APIs too?

I think that depends on what the goal of this core API is.

The GDExtension interface provides `mem_alloc` and related functions so that we can allocate memory through Godot, allowing it to be allocated in the same way as everything else in Godot and can do the same tracking. This just gives an unaligned block of memory, which can be used by GDExtension however it wants, including implementing it's own logic for using an aligned portion of it.

Do we want to "standardize" how aligned memory is allocated and track it in a special way? If so, then we probably want to add this to the GDExtension interface and encourage all language bindings to use it in this case. Or, if this was just a utility created to make it easier to allocate aligned memory for super specific use cases in rendering and physics, then we should leave it up to the bindings to implement allocating aligned memory themselves (if they want to) and we only need `mem_alloc` in the GDExtension interface. (In this 2nd case, it's arguable that this maybe should never have been added to `memory.h` and could have been kept locally in the physics and rendering subsystems.)

> Or if we need fast allocations, would those rather use language-specific allocators or allocator schemes (e.g. arenas/pools)? The latter could bypass FFI overhead and adapt to the language itself (Swift e.g. uses ref-counting, while Kotlin/C# have a GC).

I personally think it's fine for GDExtensions to allocate memory in their own way as well. However, that would mean it isn't tracked by anything in Godot (which I think I remember a recent PR removing the existing counters, with a plan to maybe add them back in another PR, so I don't think we actually are tracking it right now anyway)

Actually, I think there's a bit of misconception about why one would want aligned dynamically allocated memory for vectorization.  It's not related to arenas or pools or other allocation methods because the goal isn't in the speed or efficiency of the allocation itself.   In fact, my extension is only allocating once when the "length" and "resolution" of the simulation are known.  

The goal of aligned memory allocation is to allow the compiler to make more optimizations when vectorizing loops.  For example, if compiling a vectorizable loop (no dependence on other indices, few branches, etc), to use 128 bit SIMD registers the memory needs to be aligned to the nearest 16 bytes for the compiler to use those instructions.  This can be done with stack variables using the `alignas(16)` keyword.  Unfortunately, there is no equivalent if you want to heap allocate an array at run time.  In my case, I'm trying to target 256 bit SIMD instructions to get a throughput of 8 floats or 4 doubles per loop.  That requires 32 byte alignment.  I could have simply done the alignment myself, true, but I figured since the engine has it already, why not expose it to extensions (or implement it in godot-cpp).  

Other languages such as C# also have ways of vectorization with alignment, and I believe this would help enable more optimizations for them as well.

As a side note, this optimization could be applied to many more areas of the engine in general.  SIMD instructions don't necessarily need to be explicitly used in C++, as long as the loop meets vectorization requirements and the memory is aligned (and sometimes restricted is required).  I think either a new template for Vector (or template argument) to use these features may see great speedup in some hot loops when compiling on platforms that have SIMD instructions.

Edit: To be clear, if it's not necessary to track aligned memory separately or expose it over the interface for any other reason, I'm fine with just using an extension side implementation instead of exposing the engine side.  It may even help the compiler more if it knows the address of allocated memory is being force to certain boundaries.
